hints: Look carefully at the right-hand side of Fig. 6.2. What is collecting inside the inverted measuring cylinder as the reaction happens?
Progress means rate, so you need a change in amount with time. What two things must you record together at regular intervals?
walkthrough:
Spot which product you can see**
From Fig. 6.1, $2H_2O_2 \rightarrow 2H_2O + O_2$. Water stays in the flask, but oxygen is a gas. In Fig. 6.2 the delivery tube carries that gas into an inverted measuring cylinder full of water, so the gas bubbles up and pushes water out. The scale on the cylinder lets you read the gas volume in $cm^3$.

Turn one reading into progress over time**
One volume on its own tells you little. Record the volume at regular times, for example every 30 s, using a stopwatch. As the reaction proceeds the collected volume increases, and the increase in volume per unit time gives the rate. Plotting volume against time gives a progress curve.
Final answer: Measure the volume of oxygen gas collected in the inverted measuring cylinder / volume of water displaced, at regular time intervals.

hints: The total mass of potato is the same in both experiments, but three large pieces become six small pieces. What happens to total surface area exposed to the hydrogen peroxide?
Think about where catalase is. How does cutting open more cells change how much enzyme can meet substrate at the start?
walkthrough:
Compare surface area**
Three pieces of $20 mm \times 10 mm \times 10 mm$ cut in half give six pieces of $10 mm \times 10 mm \times 10 mm$. Same total volume of tissue, but much larger total surface area in contact with $H_2O_2$ solution.

Link surface to enzyme availability and rate**
Catalase is inside potato cells. Cutting damages more cells and exposes more enzyme directly to substrate. That means a higher effective concentration of catalase and more free active sites at the surface. More collisions lead to more enzyme-substrate complexes per unit time, so oxygen is produced faster in the second experiment.

Final answer: Smaller pieces have a larger total surface area; more cells cut open so more catalase released / higher effective enzyme concentration, so more active sites available, more enzyme-substrate complexes formed per unit time and faster rate of oxygen production.

hints: Think of the two opposing effects as temperature rises: faster molecular movement at first, then breaking of bonds in the enzyme at high temperature. What shape does that combination give?
walkthrough:
Sketch the classic optimum curve**
Start low at low temperature, rise to a peak at the optimum temperature, then drop sharply back toward zero. The rise is gradual because higher temperature means higher kinetic energy, more collisions and more enzyme-substrate complexes. The fall is steep because above the optimum hydrogen bonds break, the active site changes shape and catalase is denatured, so rate falls rapidly.
Final answer: Curve rises gradually to an optimum then falls steeply to zero.
